newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Rosgosstrakh sees premium tripled in 7 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Russia Rosgosstrakh sees premium tripled in 7 yrs.

text.p: Russia's biggest insurance company, OAO Rosgosstrakh, hopes to triple premiums in seven years from about three trillion roubles in 1996, Chairman Vladislav Reznik said on Thursday.
The growth will be due to new products in life insurance and improved agents' work, he told Reuters.
The key element in this -- financing -- will come as a result of the company's privatisation now in progress, he said.

Although all proceeds from the sale will go to the state, Reznik hopes investors will buy shares from new issues attracted by high dividends, while foreign investors can supply the company with know-how.
He said he hoped the World Bank could advise Rosgosstrakh on organising the sale of its shares abroad.
"We are counting on investors," he said. "We need shareholders. If we have one million shareholders it will mean we have one million new clients."
The Russian Federal Property Fund will sell 50 percent of Rosgosstrakh at a cash auction at a price of 500 rouble per share with nominal value of two roubles this year.
Under Rosgosstrakh's privatisation scheme, 20 percent of shares have been sold to employees at 10.52 roubles each.
Reznik said a nine-member group headed by Reznik has a priority right to buy a further 30 percent at 10.52 roubles each in a deal to be signed in July.
New shareholders will help the company increase authorised capital, he said.
Rosgosstrakh's capital already exceeds the new minimum laid down by a bill going through the State Duma lower house of parliament, but this could be raised further.
The draft law, passed in the first reading, calls for an insurer's minimum authorised capital to rise to $250,000 from the current minimum of two million roubles ($350).
Rosgosstrakh's authorised capital is 2.1 billion roubles ($350,000 at the current exchange rate), according to 1994 calculations.
Rosgosstrakh's privatisation has come under fire from the Duma, which thinks its assets of 11 billion roubles have been undervalued and has asked the Audit Chamber to investigate.
The chamber plans to finish the probe by the end of the week.
The Moscow Arbitration Court has also suspended the privatisation pending a suit from the union of depositors at state savings bank Sberbank, until the court sits on March 25.
Reznik defended the scheme under which his nine-member group, called Rosgosstrakh-Trust, gets the right to buy 30 percent of the company.
Many privatisations of Russian companies have resulted in the management getting large or even controlling stakes.
"There may be no effective management if it does not have an interest in the results," he said.
The management headed by Reznik came to Rosgosstrakh in 1995 and raised its market share in voluntary insurance to 17 percent from 15.4 percent.

They centralised finances in Rosgosstrakh's 80 affiliates and tightened controls over their activities, Reznik said. Out of 46 loss-making affiliates, 22 are now profitable and improvements are underway at the rest.
Rosgosstrakh's 1996 premiums rose to a preliminary 3.09 trillion roubles from 2.70 trillion roubles in 1995.
